new_statements.quote: In Arakanese Burmese a phonological word carries only one main (strong) stress. The stress is placed on the last syllable of a phonological word. That is : a strongly stressed syllable shows the end of a phonological word. Thus a phonological word in this study is a stress group as well. [p.17] ... In Arakanese Burmese, stress is predictable from the type of syllables and its position in a phonological word. Therefore word stress need not to be mentioned overtly at the phonemic level. [p.43] ... The nuclear syllable is a major syllable and always takes strong stress. It always occupies the last position in the word. [p.46]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive, predictable word stress: each phonological word (= stress group) has exactly one strong (primary) stress, on its final syllable, which is always a full 'major' syllable carrying tone; non-final syllables are either 'minor' (full vowel + tone, weak stress) or 'presyllables' (Cə, reduced schwa, neutral tone, zero stress). Stress defined as intensity plus vowel duration; tone is the lexical contrast (4 tones).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Weak (secondary) stress [,] falls on any non-final 'minor' syllable (full vowel with tone); presyllables (Cə with neutral tone) and, in tri-/tetrasyllables, some minor syllables carry zero stress. Patterns listed pp.17-22, e.g. disyllables [z.'s] or [,w.'s]; trisyllables [z.,w.'s], [,w.z.'s], [z.z.'s], [,w.,w.'s].
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; monosyllables 'usually' carry the strong stress; compound words treated separately (sec. 3.3). Author notes stress need not be marked phonemically because it is fully predictable.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word defined as a stress group within the intonation group; word = citation forms of 1-4 syllables (most words monosyllabic). Variety: Arakanese (Rakhine) of Sittwe city; tonal language (4 tones) with a stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: arak1256 'Arakanese' (ISO mhv) is a retired bookkeeping code, split in 2008 into Rakhine [rki] = rakh1245 (Myanmar) and Marma [rmz] = marm1234 (Bangladesh). The quoted source describes Arakanese as spoken in Sittwe city, Rakhine State, Myanmar, i.e. Rakhine rakh1245 (Glottolog files the thesis under rki). For the Marma half only tone/weak-syllable descriptions were found (Huziwara 2003), no stress rule. A parallel our files for rakh1245 already holds Okell 1995, Bradley 1985, Huziwara 2003 etc; the Rungjit thesis found here also serves rakh1245.

sources.note: Ch. III sec. 3.1 p.17: a phonological word carries one main (strong) stress, placed on the LAST syllable; sec. 3.2 pp.17-22 lists stress patterns for 1-4-syllable words, all ending in strong stress; sec. 4.2.2 pp.43-45: stress (intensity + vowel duration) is predictable from syllable type and position, three degrees strong ['] on the major (final) syllable, weak/secondary [,] on minor syllables, zero on presyllables (Ca with reduced schwa, neutral tone); sec. 4.3.1 p.46: nuclear syllable = major syllable, always strong-stressed, always word-final.

sources.note: Arakanese outline phonology sec. 2.2: tone inventory heavy/creaky/low/stop plus 'weak'; sec. 2.3.2.2 Weakening pp.16-17: AR weakens (reduces to schwa) first syllables of compounds more extensively than Standard Burmese. The word 'stress' is not used for Arakanese.

sources.citation: Huziwara, Keisuke. 2003. マルマ語の音声に関する考察 [A phonetic analysis of Marma]. 京都大学言語学研究 22: 237-300.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Marma (Rajasthali, CHT): sec. 2.5 four tones (low, high, rising, high-checked) plus a non-distinctive 軽声 'light tone' on Cə syllables (Cə.CV); sec. 2.6.2 first element of CVCV compounds often realised Cə. Only mention of 強勢 'stress' is in the summary of D. Bernot 1958's description of tone 2 (strong syllable-initial stress). No word-stress rule.

sources.note: p.189: a shwa with no tonal contrast marks a reduced syllable; Burmese and Arakanese words have one reduced syllable in a two-syllable word, the first or second or first two in a three-syllable word; Arakanese reduces nasal-final syllables less than Burmese. No statement using 'stress'.
